title: Number of Nodes With Value One
statement:
A tree holds `n` nodes labeled `1` through `n`. Node `1` is the root, and every other node `v` hangs below node `floor(v / 2)`, so node `v` has children `2v` and `2v + 1` whenever those labels are at most `n`.

Every node starts with the value `0`. Process `queries` in order: for each entry `queries[i]`, toggle the value (`0` becomes `1`, `1` becomes `0`) of every node in the subtree rooted at node `queries[i]`, including that node itself.

Return how many nodes have the value `1` after all the queries are done.
notes:
## Intuition

A node's final value depends only on how many queries hit it or one of its ancestors: each such query toggles it once. Simulating every query over its whole subtree can cost O(n) per query. Instead, record for each node whether it was queried an odd number of times, then walk the tree once from the root, carrying the parity of toggles collected along the path.

## Approach

1. Build `flipped`, where `flipped[v]` is `1` if `v` appears an odd number of times in `queries` (XOR each hit in). Two toggles at the same node cancel.
2. Run `dfs(node, parity)`, where `parity` is the XOR of `flipped` over the node's proper ancestors.
3. A label past `n` is not in the tree, so it contributes `0`.
4. The node's own `value` is `parity ^ flipped[node]`; pass it down to children `2 * node` and `2 * node + 1`.
5. Return `value` plus the counts from both subtrees; the answer is `dfs(1, 0)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 5`, `queries = [1, 2, 5]`, so `flipped` marks nodes 1, 2 and 5. `dfs(1, 0)` gives node 1 `value = 1`. Node 2 gets `1 ^ 1 = 0`; its children 4 and 5 get `0 ^ 0 = 0` and `0 ^ 1 = 1`. Node 3 gets `1 ^ 0 = 1`. The ones are nodes 1, 3 and 5, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + q): one pass over `queries`, then each node is visited once.
- Space: O(n) for `flipped`; the recursion is only about log2(n) ≈ 17 deep because the tree is complete.

## Pitfalls

- Toggling every subtree per query is O(n · q), far too slow at 10^5 each.
- Repeated queries on the same node cancel in pairs; counting them with `+` instead of parity gives wrong values.
- Stop at labels greater than `n`: the last level of the tree may be only partly filled.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `flipped` | `flipped[v]` is 1 when node `v` was queried an odd number of times |
| `node` | label of the node being visited |
| `parity` | toggles (mod 2) inherited from the node's ancestors |
| `value` | the node's final value |
| `left`, `right` | number of ones in the left and right subtrees |

narration.2: One slot per label; it will hold whether that node was toggled an odd number of times.
narration.4: XOR in the hit, so two queries on the same node cancel.
narration.7: dfs returns the number of ones in the subtree of node, given the parity inherited from its ancestors.
narration.8: A label beyond n is not part of the tree.
narration.9: An empty subtree has no ones.
narration.11: The node's final value is the inherited parity toggled by its own queries.
narration.12: Count the ones in the left child's subtree, passing this node's value down.
narration.13: Do the same for the right child.
narration.14: This node's value plus both subtree counts.
narration.17: Start at the root, which has no ancestors, so the inherited parity is 0.
